Al-Durr reports recitation at Umm Kulthūm's burial with 'In God's name, in God's path, and upon the way of God's Messenger.' Study Quran says Muslims often recite it at funerals."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q01", "question": "Why does Moses' speech begin here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q01/p1", "position": "It resumes the scene after Pharaoh gathered his forces, leaving Moses' arrival understood and showing him open the contest with counsel.", "reasons": "Bursevi and al-Alusi say the wording answers the implicit question of what Moses did next; al-Alusi says his arrival needs no repetition. Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise calls it an explanatory beginning. Islāhī places the speech first in the public arena."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q02", "question": "Whom does 'them' address?", "turns_on": "Whether the implied magicians alone supply the plural antecedent, or the prior gathering and public audience include Pharaoh and his party.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q02/p1", "position": "The sorcerers assembled by Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī links them to Pharaoh's gathering of his stratagem at 20:60; Ibn al-Jawzī points to his discussion at 7:114. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the promised matching magic implies them and says an actual imprecation could target them alone, preserving gentle speech to Pharaoh."}, {"id": "20:61/q02/p2", "position": "Pharaoh, the sorcerers, and others present or assisting him.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī names Pharaoh and magicians; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the court could hear and see and the assembled scheme implies them. Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes Pharaoh, his schemes, magicians, and helpers, arguing that magicians alone had not been mentioned previously."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q03", "question": "How many sorcerers were gathered?", "turns_on": "The reports give different counts, while one view specifies only a large gathering.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q03/p1", "position": "Seventy-two, each carrying a rope and staff.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī gives this report."}, {"id": "20:61/q03/p2", "position": "Four hundred.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī reports this as another account."}, {"id": "20:61/q03/p3", "position": "Twelve thousand or more.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī attributes this to Kaʿb."}, {"id": "20:61/q03/p4", "position": "They were numerous, without a specified count.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this as another view alongside the miracle and sleight-of-hand distinction."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q04", "question": "What was Moses doing by this warning, and how did the sorcerers respond?", "turns_on": "The notes describe successive sides of the encounter rather than competing histories.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q04/p1", "position": "He admonished and intimidated them, calling them to God and the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī names admonition and intimidation. Al-Qushayrī says Moses exhausted gentleness, offered warning of punishment and promise of grace, and spoke of afterlife reward and punishment."}, {"id": "20:61/q04/p2", "position": "They dismissed his warning and miracle as falsehood and magic and alleged that he and Aaron sought their expulsion and the destruction of their way.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts Moses' counsel with Pharaoh's folly and their worldly response; his reminders increased their heedlessness."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q05", "question": "What does 'woe to you' convey?", "turns_on": "Whether waylakum functions chiefly as an imprecation and rebuke or an exclamation of astonishment.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q05/p1", "position": "A warning, rebuke, or invocation of ruin and punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says it threatens that God impose woe; Bursevī says the original invocation now restrains fabrication; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it a threat of punishment. Ibn ʿĀshūr says wayl names punishment or evil and has no verb. Al-Qurṭubī calls it an invocation of woe."}, {"id": "20:61/q05/p2", "position": "An expression of astonishment at their strange conduct, with a warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the Prophet's astonished description of Abū Baṣīr as a fire-stirrer of war; he gives no grading for the report. Al-Ṭabrisī also reports an analysis as wonder."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q06", "question": "How is 'woe to you' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether its accusative depends on an implied verb or an omitted vocative particle.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q06/p1", "position": "An accusative verbal noun or object governed by an understood verb imposing woe.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, through al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī, supplies the implied imposition of woe. Al-Qurṭubī calls it a verbal noun. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows an omitted warning or exhortation verb, referring to 2:79."}, {"id": "20:61/q06/p2", "position": "An accusative vocative with an omitted calling particle.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and those transmitting him compare 36:52; he also cites 19:4, and al-Rāzī's account mentions 11:72. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 2:79. Al-Ṭabrisī reports an invocation of woe and says it may be analyzed as two words."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q07", "question": "How can the sharp 'woe' fit the command to speak gently to Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "Whether Pharaoh is addressed, whether the phrase curses, and whether the circumstances permitted forceful speech.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q07/p1", "position": "It may address only the sorcerers, leaving Pharaoh outside the imprecation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr makes this conditional on waylakum being a genuine imprecation."}, {"id": "20:61/q07/p2", "position": "Moses may have received special leave to speak harshly after Pharaoh's settled disbelief resisted gentleness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the restriction of a general command with Muhammad's permission to fight at 22:39."}, {"id": "20:61/q07/p3", "position": "The sorcerers' public misleading made forceful denunciation fitting.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says they invoked Pharaoh's might as evidence of divine support before the crowd."}, {"id": "20:61/q07/p4", "position": "The phrase can express astonishment rather than an imprecation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the Prophet's expression to Abū Baṣīr as a parallel, without grading the report."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q08", "question": "What lie against God does Moses forbid?", "turns_on": "Which act in the contest is the intended fabrication: denying the signs, presenting magic as divine, or claiming divinity for others; several authors include multiple acts.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q08/p1", "position": "Calling Moses' genuine signs, message, or proof sorcery and denying their divine origin.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies the hand and staff; al-Wāḥidī reports the same. Al-Rāzī says this claim licenses opposition; Ibn ʿAṭiyya stresses knowingly opposing recognized truth. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes Pharaoh's political-intrigue label; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes calling Moses liar and magician. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates 5:103, and Study Quran 10:77."}, {"id": "20:61/q08/p2", "position": "Presenting their sorcery or illusions as divine truth or a genuine miracle.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says they attribute magic to God. Ibn Kathīr says illusions falsely suggest real creation and thus attribute creation to God. Al-Taʾwīlāt, quoted by Bursevī, says they claim the prophetic gift for their magic. Ibn ʿĀshūr mentions ropes made to seem snakes and claimed divine backing. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī includes magic presented as mere magic."}, {"id": "20:61/q08/p3", "position": "Associating partners with God or treating Pharaoh or other gods as divine.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported by al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn al-Jawzī. Islāhī locates the debate in Pharaoh's claim to divinity: the true Lord creates and sustains, while alleged partners have no revealed proof. Ṭabāṭabāʾī specifies claims of divinity, intercession and control of the world, citing 7:89. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes Pharaoh and his gods."}, {"id": "20:61/q08/p4", "position": "Deliberately attributing any falsehood to God or denying His messages.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī states the general prohibition; Ibn ʿAṭiyya emphasizes knowing the truth. Asad construes it as deliberate denial of God's messages; Ibn ʿĀshūr lists the several forms their blasphemous claims took. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says Pharaoh's labels severed the signs from God."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q09", "question": "What does the expression 'fabricate a lie' add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q09/p1", "position": "Iftirāʾ is deliberate invention of falsehood; adding 'a lie' emphasizes it.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba equates fabrication with lying; Bursevī stresses deliberateness. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the cognate sense emphatic and compares 5:103."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q10", "question": "What does 'He will eradicate you' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the gloss emphasizes total removal and death or the hardship inflicted by punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q10/p1", "position": "God will destroy them utterly, removing every trace.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says no remnant remains; Qatāda says they are cut off completely. Al-Layth and language scholars relate the root to shaving hair close; Islāhī gives peeling meat from bone and later uprooting or exploitation. Abū ʿUbayda, Abū ʿUthmān, al-Zajjāj and others treat saḥata and asḥata as equivalent. Al-Farazdaq's depleted-wealth line, also cited with Suwayd by Abū ʿUbayda, illustrates removal; its transmitted spelling and case vary. Al-Farrāʾ says yusḥitu is common. Al-Rāzī, al-Biqāʿī and others stress complete extermination."}, {"id": "20:61/q10/p2", "position": "God will wear them down to the utmost hardship by punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAṭāʾ uses 'wear down'; al-Layth gives utmost hardship and recognizes

 asḥatnāhum as a dialect form."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q11", "question": "How is 'He will eradicate you' read?", "turns_on": "The two accepted dialectal verb forms and reader transmissions; most sources equate their meanings, while Qirāʾāt-ER distinguishes direct action from causation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q11/p1", "position": "With fatḥa on yāʾ and ḥāʾ, from the triliteral saḥata, the Hijazi form.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir; reports also add Ibn ʿAbbās, Ruways and Ibn Abāʿī in their respective enumerations. Al-Ṭabarī prefers this as more eloquent highland usage; al-Naḥḥās also prefers the Hijazi form. Al-Farrāʾ is reported elsewhere as calling the other form more common. Both generally mean destruction; Qirāʾāt-ER distinguishes this as God's direct scraping or destruction. Some reports abbreviate the reader lists."}, {"id": "20:61/q11/p2", "position": "With ḍamma on yāʾ and kasra on ḥāʾ, from quadriliteral asḥata, the Najdi or Tamimi form.", "reasons": "The usual list is Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim; later lists add Khalaf, Ruways, Yaʿqūb, al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa or Ibn Jarīr. Al-Rāzī's summary names ʿĀṣim without distinguishing transmitters. Al-Farazdaq's masḥatan is cited for this form, though its verse's parsing is disputed. Al-Ṭabarī calls both correct and Ibn ʿĀshūr both eloquent. Qirāʾāt-ER distinguishes Form IV as causing destruction through an intermediary."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q12", "question": "Why is the verb after the prohibition in the subjunctive?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q12/p1", "position": "It gives the consequence of the prohibition, with an implicit an after fa.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, al-Qurṭubī and al-Nasafī call it the answer or result of 'do not fabricate'; al-Samīn explicitly supplies an elided an governing the accusative."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q13", "question": "How is al-Farazdaq's cited line parsed?", "turns_on": "Different transmissions and explanations of the raised masḥat and mujallaf in the poem.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q13/p1", "position": "In one transmission, masḥatan denotes what remains after loss, and raised mujallaf is coordinated with it.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn describes masḥatan as quasi-subject of 'nothing remained'; he says al-Zamakhsharī cites the construction for raised qalīl at 2:249. Al-Farazdaq's text is transmitted with masḥatan or masḥat, with Abū ʿUbayda giving nominative case; al-Kashshāf and al-Qurṭubī note sustained dispute."}, {"id": "20:61/q13/p2", "position": "Raised mujallaf has an omitted verb: 'or some stripped remnant remained.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn supplies baqiya from the preceding lam yadaʿ."}, {"id": "20:61/q13/p3", "position": "Raised mujallaf is a subject with an omitted predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports al-Farrāʾ's estimate 'or mujallaf likewise'."}, {"id": "20:61/q13/p4", "position": "Mujallaf is coordinated with the concealed pronoun in masḥatan.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports al-Kisāʾī's view: separation is ordinarily expected, but he does not require it and poetry permits the coordination."}, {"id": "20:61/q13/p5", "position": "Mujallaf is a verbal noun shaped like a passive participle and coordinated with 'the bite of time'.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports al-Fārisī's analogy to mumazzaq at 34:19 and expressly prefers this fifth analysis."}, {"id": "20:61/q13/p6", "position": "With kasra on dāl, masḥat is raised as subject of active wadaʿ, with mujallaf coordinated.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports a second transmission and an omitted pronoun meaning 'because of it'."}, {"id": "20:61/q13/p7", "position": "With passive yudaʿ, masḥat is the deputy subject and mujallaf is coordinated.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this third transmission; he says the wāw should remain in the passive because it is not between yāʾ and kasra, so its deletion follows analogy with the active form. He refers to fuller discussion under al-Baqara."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q14", "question": "What punishment does the warning threaten?", "turns_on": "Al-Rāzī leaves the threatened punishment open between worldly annihilation and severe punishment in the Hereafter.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q14/p1", "position": "A devastating annihilation or uprooting in this world.", "reasons": "The verb's eradication sense supplies the force; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the indefinite 'punishment' marks severity and shirk brings annihilation. Bursevī and al-Alūsī describe the torment as immense and beyond measure. Asad calls it grievous suffering; Islāhī says false attribution makes them liable, as wrongdoers are."}, {"id": "20:61/q14/p2", "position": "Severe punishment in the Hereafter may be intended.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī offers this as an alternative to worldly annihilation."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q15", "question": "Who is the failed fabricator?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative man is taken in full generality, applied to shirk, or directed to Pharaoh as an immediate example.", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q15/p1", "position": "Anyone who invents a lie against God; the rule is general.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says man is general, and al-Alūsī stresses any manner of fabrication. Bursevī says whoever and however. Al-Biqāʿī extends deliberate lying even to lies against others. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this is broader than 16:116 and recalls Joseph's falsely bloodied shirt at 12:18. The specific prohibited fabrication remains its immediate instance."}, {"id": "20:61/q15/p2", "position": "The person who claims another deity beside God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is quoted by al-Wāḥidī; al-Wāḥidī's concise commentary also makes the fabricator a claimant of another deity."}, {"id": "20:61/q15/p3", "position": "Pharaoh in particular, whose fabrication failed to preserve his rule.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī applies it to Pharaoh's unsuccessful schemes. Al-Alūsī offers Pharaoh as an alternative intended referent, warning the sorcerers not to share his frustration."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q16", "question": "What is the fabricator's failure?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q16/p1", "position": "Loss of the desired outcome, ultimately deprivation of divine mercy, reward, and Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says loss and deprivation of God's reward; al-Ṭabrisī reports Qatāda's 'lost' and another account's lost hope of reward and Paradise. Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī specify lost mercy and reward. Abū Ḥayyān and Bursevī define khayba as missing one's aim; al-Rāzī adds deprivation of one's aim. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says false causes cannot yield true lasting good; Asad calls the liar already doomed."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q17", "question": "How does the closing sentence support Moses' warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q17/p1", "position": "It gives a general reason for the ban and reinforces it as a parenthetical statement.", "reasons": "Al-Alūsī calls it parenthetical; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it circumstantial and the major premise of a categorical syllogism, with earlier fabricators' failure as evidence. Moses thereby signals he would not falsely claim revelation, knowing God would destroy a fabricator."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q18", "question": "What rhetorical device links the verse's beginning and ending?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q18/p1", "position": "Taṣdīr, or returning the ending to the beginning, repeats the fabrication root.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī identifies the return and compares 17:21. Al-Suyūṭī defines taṣdīr and reports Ibn al-Muʿtazz's three forms: the end matches the last, first, or another opening word; he assigns this verse's final iftarā to the earlier taftarū. Al-Zarkashī lists further examples at 42:20, 21:37, 9:104, 9:70, 6:31, 71:10, 33:37, 5:12 and 9:112."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q19", "question": "What role can poetic amplification play at a verse ending?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q19/p1", "position": "Some seek īghāl at Qur'anic verse endings, as a rhyme may heighten a complete meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī cites poets' extreme praise, reaching beyond sun or sky, then notes that Imruʾ al-Qays's rhyme adds description although the sense stands without it; his discussion treats īghāl as a poetic device sought by some only at verse endings."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q20", "question": "What makes their denial especially blameworthy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q20/p1", "position": "Rejecting a witnessed miracle after proof is graver and warrants greater punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the open daylight gathering displayed the miracle to all, whereas sleight of hand often works privately, at night, or on the ignorant; Moses' challenge exposed the difference."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q21", "question": "What does accountability in this warning imply about human acts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q21/p1", "position": "People produce their own acts and can justly be punished for denial and turning away.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī argues otherwise God's signs, attributing denial and turning away to people, and punishing them for those acts would make no sense."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q22", "question": "Why did the sorcerers fail to benefit from the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q22/p1", "position": "Their inward blindness and divine exclusion left them heedless of faith, grace, and the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says open warning did not reach their inward perception; they answered only in worldly terms, and reminders increased ignorance. One marked by exclusion has no gnosis or faith, regrets nothing missed, and disbelieves what lies ahead."}]}
{"id": "20:61/q23", "question": "What drew the sorcerers into the contest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:61/q23/p1", "position": "They sought reward and rank from Pharaoh, with inducements or threats pressing them to face Moses.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī refers to Pharaoh's promise of payment and closeness in 26:41–42."}]}

 gives this exhortation?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing clause continues the contestants' speech or is an inserted divine judgment, and whether Pharaoh or the sorcerers address the group.", "positions": [{"id": "20:64/q01/p1", "position": "The magicians exhort one another, including the closing claim.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī and Asad present mutual urging; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī call this the apparent reading. {"id": "20:64/q02", "question": "How is فَأَجْمِعُوا۟ read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted hamza and mīm vowels, and whether 20:60 supports repetition of 'gather' or favors a new command to resolve.", "positions": [{"id": "20:64/q02/p1", "position": "Most readers use a cut hamza and kasra on mīm, fa-ajmiʿū, from ajmaʿa.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid, Abū ʿAlī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Nashr and Ibn ʿĀshūr report the majority reading. Al-Qaṭʿī and Hārūn also transmit it from Abū ʿAmr. It commonly means firm resolve; some allow gathering too. Abū al-Ḥasan says the cut form is more widely read; Abū ʿAlī allows dialectal Form I/Form IV alternation."}, {"id": "20:64/q02/p2", "position": "Abū ʿAmr and other transmitted readers use a joined hamza and fatḥa on mīm, fajmaʿū, from jamaʿa.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr is the standard attribution; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī add al-Zuhrī, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Yaʿqūb in one route, and Abū Ḥātim. The wording فجمع كيده at 20:60 is cited for it, though Muḥammad ibn Yazīd argues the earlier gathering makes the distinct sense 'resolve' preferable. Al-Akhfash prefers this form for collecting."}]}
{"id": "20:64/q03", "question": "What does the command فَأَجْمِعُوا۟ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the command evokes firm joint resolve or the collecting of available stratagems; some authorities allow both verbs to overlap.", "positions": [{"id": "20:64/q03/p1", "position": "Settle the plan decisively and agree on it together.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and others say unanimity prevents division and failure. Al-Farrāʾ illustrates firm resolution with 'I resolved to travel'; poetic mujmaʿ means a settled affair. Al-Rāghib describes ijmāʿ as collecting after deliberation. Al-Ālūsī cites Abū al-Haytham: making an affair one after wavering. Ibn Hishām associates ajmaʿa with abstract matters; ʿUmdat al-Ḥuffāẓ says this is usual but reversible. Al-Muḥkam and Abū ʿAlī permit overlap of the two forms."}, {"id": "20:64/q03/p2", "position": "Collect, marshal and bring forward every stratagem and instrument of magic.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says marshal the plots; Muqātil and Yaḥyā connect them with magic. Al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ say leave no trick unused. 20:60's فجمع كيده is cited for the connected reading; al-Nahhās accepts this despite the previous gathering. Al-Aṣmaʿī distinguishes bringing things from places from forming a single whole; al-Farrāʾ distinguishes gathering people and money. Abū Dhuʾayb's verse about gathered booty and a Hudhalī line support collection; al-Thaʿlabī allows the cut form this meaning too."}]}
{"id": "20:64/q04", "question": "What is the magicians' كَيْدَكُمْ?", "turns_on": "Whether the plot is described by its magical means or its larger public purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "20:64/q04/p1", "position": "Their sorcery, tricks, and means for defeating Moses and Aaron.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Yaḥyā identify it as magic; al-Thaʿlabī adds deceit and expertise, al-Nasafī its instruments, and Ibn Kathīr says they would cast all at once to dazzle eyes and overwhelm the prophets."}, {"id": "20:64/q04/p2", "position": "A coordinated public deception to make Moses' sign seem like ordinary magic and protect the regime's way of life.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says they planned to match or exceed the sign so its distinctive force vanished before a perplexed public; 26:38–40 depicts assembly and calls to attend. {"id": "20:64/q05", "question": "How is كَيْدَكُمْ governed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the object is directly governed, follows a new phrase, or depends on an unspoken ʿalā.", "positions": [{"id": "20:64/q05/p1", "position": "It is the verb's direct object.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn explicitly parses kaydakum as a direct object and dismisses an elided preposition."}, {"id": "20:64/q05/p2", "position": "The resolve command may be complete, with كيدكم beginning a new phrase.", "reasons": "Abū al-Ḥasan, as reported by al-Ṭabrisī, allows understanding 'agree on it' before a new phrase about their plot; he also allows dialect variation between the forms."}, {"id": "20:64/q05/p3", "position": "It follows an omitted preposition ʿalā.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this alternative only to reject it."}]}

{"id": "20:68/q01", "question": "What events or means of delivery are reported around God's reassurance?", "turns_on": "The reports give different surrounding events or modes of communication.", "positions": [{"id": "20:68/q01/p1", "position": "Gabriel conveyed God's assurance to Moses.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies Gabriel as its conveyor and compares the promised victory with 3:139 and 47:35."}, {"id": "20:68/q01/p2", "position": "The reassurance came as immediate revelation.", "reasons": "Islahi says this revelation restored Moses' confidence despite the apparent depth of the magicians' spectacle."}, {"id": "20:68/q01/p3", "position": "Moses disputed Gabriel's call for gentleness toward the magicians before Gabriel foretold their imminent conversion and Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports Moses' objection that the magicians sought to defeat the miracle and support Pharaoh's religion; Gabriel said they would be with Moses until afternoon prayer, then in Paradise."}, {"id": "20:68/q01/p4", "position": "Moses wondered whether God's knowledge of his eventual state might differ from his present state, as with the magicians; God then reassured him.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi gives the change in the magicians' state as the comparison."}]}
{"id": "20:68/q02", "question": "What fear of Moses does 'Do not fear' address?", "turns_on": "The notes locate the fear in apparent magic, concern for the people, a question about divine knowledge, or an inward encounter with divine power; some describe human fear without specifying its object.", "positions": [{"id": "20:68/q02/p1", "p

osition": "He feared the magicians' impressive magic might seem to prevail or lead the public astray.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas says the apparent confusion would be resolved by proof; al-Biqa'i says God could nullify their magic; al-Alusi describes an imagined danger; Ibn Ashur says he feared even a temporary public impression of defeat, despite confidence in his mission, citing 3:196–197 for possible temporary unbeliever success; the Ibn Atiyye report in Kuran Yolu says the spectacle briefly affected Moses and raised fear for the people; Islahi notes how profound the magic seemed."}, {"id": "20:68/q02/p2", "position": "He feared for his people's loss of their share of God, rather than for himself.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata, as reported by al-Alusi, explains the fear as concern that the people would lose their divine share."}, {"id": "20:68/q02/p3", "position": "He feared the Creator manifested in the serpent's overpowering of magic, not his created staff.", "reasons": "The inward reading in al-Bursevi says Moses recognized God's overpowering attribute in the serpent swallowing the magic."}, {"id": "20:68/q02/p4", "position": "He wondered whether God's knowledge of his destiny differed from his present state.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi compares the magicians' changed state; the reassurance followed this concern."}, {"id": "20:68/q02/p5", "position": "He felt an inward human fear that required divine reassurance.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Sallam says the fear was inward; the inward reading transmitted by al-Bursevi says fear belongs to human nature even in a prophet until God removes it by command."}]}
{"id": "20:68/q03", "question": "What does the command 'Do not fear' do?", "turns_on": "Al-Alusi contrasts a literal prohibition with the reported reading of the command as encouragement.", "positions": [{"id": "20:68/q03/p1", "position": "It literally tells Moses to stop the fear that had overtaken him.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the prohibition is literal and addresses the imagined danger."}, {"id": "20:68/q03/p2", "position": "It heartens Moses and removes his fear.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi says the reassurance steadied him; al-Qashani attributes the strengthening to the Holy Spirit; an opinion reported by al-Alusi reads the command as encouragement; al-Tabatabai says it supports him because the magicians' trick cannot harm one superior to them in every respect; Kuran Yolu says it raised Moses' morale."}]}
{"id": "20:68/q04", "question": "Why can Moses be assured that he need not fear?", "turns_on": "The notes explain the assurance through God's protective presence and through the promised outcome of the contest.", "positions": [{"id": "20:68/q04/p1", "position": "God accompanies, sees, protects, and empowers him against the magicians' merely material means.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata in al-Sulami invokes God's seeing and hearing and contrasts reliance on the Causer with reliance on causes; al-Biqa'i says God's presence enables Him to nullify the magic; al-Bursevi adds divine signs protecting Moses in every state; Ibn Ata in al-Alusi offers divine care as one explanation of 'uppermost'; al-Qashani describes strengthening through the Holy Spirit."}, {"id": "20:68/q04/p2", "position": "His superiority and coming victory make the magicians' trick powerless.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai says Moses is superior in every respect, so their trick cannot harm him; al-Razi says the assurance removes fear that his cause might fail to prevail; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi say the promise of victory explains the command."}]}

Yahya, al-Thalabi, al-Wahidi's Wajiz, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Bursevi, al-Alusi and Islahi likewise describe victory or dominance."}, {"id": "20:68/q05/p2", "position": "Moses will prevail here and hold the highest ranks in Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi joins worldly triumph over the magicians with the rank granted by prophethood and God's choosing Moses."}, {"id": "20:68/q05/p3", "position": "Moses is superior to the magicians in every respect.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai says this comprehensive superiority makes their trick incapable of harming him."}, {"id": "20:68/q05/p4", "position": "Moses is above his own created staff as God's messenger and chosen intimate.", "reasons": "The inward reading reported by al-Bursevi says Moses manifests divine gentleness and power, whereas the staff manifests only overpowering."}, {"id": "20:68/q05/p5", "position": "Moses is under divine care and protection.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata, reported by al-Alusi, gives this as one of two readings, the other being victory that wins followers."}]}
{"id": "20:68/q06", "question": "How does the wording make the assurance emphatic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:68/q06/p1", "position": "An independently asserted, layered affirmation makes Moses' superiority and victory certain.", "reasons": "Al-Razi cites inna, repeated pronoun, the definite article and 'higher'; al-Baydawi adds the independent assertion and superlative; al-Nasafi lists inna, anta, definiteness and superiority; Abu Hayyan adds the renewed clause; al-Biqai says the force counters the apparent might of the magic; al-Alusi describes a discourse response plus affirmation, pronoun, definite predicate and comparative; Ibn Ashur says inna, separating pronoun and definite al-a'la answer Moses' fear of apparent public defeat."}]}
